clinical: Seddon's classification grades nerve injuries by how much of the nerve is disrupted. In axonotmesis the axons are cut but the connective tissue sheaths survive, so the nerve can regrow; in neurotmesis the sheaths are severed too and surgical repair is usually needed.

Nerve fibres.description: Each nerve fibre is an axon with Schwann cells around it. In myelinated fibres one Schwann cell wraps a single axon segment in a myelin sheath, and the gaps between successive Schwann cells (nodes of Ranvier) are where the impulse is regenerated, so it jumps from node to node. Unmyelinated (C) fibres have no spiral sheath; several thin axons sit in grooves of one Schwann cell.
clinical: In Guillain-Barré syndrome the immune system attacks the myelin sheaths of peripheral nerves (in some forms the axons too), causing weakness and tingling that build over days to weeks, often after a respiratory or gut infection.
The most common form, CMT1A, is caused by an extra copy of the PMP22 gene, which leads to abnormal myelin. Nerves conduct slowly, and weakness and wasting usually start in the feet and lower legs.

Vessels.description: The blood supply of a nerve runs in two parts. Arterioles from nearby arteries form a longitudinal network in the epineurium (the vasa nervorum), and their branches pierce the perineurium to feed the endoneurial capillaries inside each fascicle. The endoneurial capillaries have tight junctions and form the vascular part of the blood-nerve barrier, and venules drain blood back out through the perineurium.
clinical: In diabetes, damage to the small vessels that supply nerves (the vasa nervorum) is one contributor to diabetic neuropathy, alongside direct metabolic injury to the nerve. The neuropathy typically starts in the feet, with numbness, tingling and pain.

In systemic vasculitis, inflammation of the vasa nervorum can block blood flow to parts of a nerve. The result is mononeuritis multiplex: painful weakness and numbness in several separate areas, each supplied by a different nerve.

parts.description: Epineurium is the dense irregular connective tissue that wraps a whole peripheral nerve and binds its fascicles into one cable. Its outer part is a tough sheath, while looser tissue between the fascicles carries fat and the vasa nervorum, the small vessels that supply the nerve. It cushions the fascicles against compression and is the layer sutured in an epineurial nerve repair. In cross-section it forms the collagen-rich outer rim of the nerve, around the separate round fascicles.

Epineurial collagen bundles are the wavy bundles of type I collagen that make up the outer epineurium and run mostly along the length of the nerve. Their gentle crimp lets the nerve lengthen a little as a joint moves, before the fascicles inside are stretched. In sections they appear as pale pink, wavy bundles with fibroblast nuclei scattered between them.

Perineurium is the layered sheath of flattened perineurial cells that wraps around each fascicle of a peripheral nerve. Each lamella has a basal lamina on both surfaces and tight junctions joining its cells, with thin collagen between the layers. It gives the fascicle tensile strength and, together with the endoneurial capillaries, forms the blood-nerve barrier that limits entry of substances from the blood. In cross-section it appears as a thin, layered pale ring with flattened nuclei round each fascicle.

Endoneurium is the loose connective tissue that fills the space between the individual nerve fibres inside a fascicle, bathed in endoneurial fluid. It contains fine collagen, fibroblasts, and a few mast cells and macrophages. After an axon is cut, the endoneurial tube it runs in, which holds the Schwann cells (the bands of Büngner), guides regrowth at about 1 mm a day. That is why axonotmesis, where the endoneurial tube stays intact, usually recovers, while neurotmesis, where the nerve is cut through, needs surgical repair.

Myelin sheaths (internodes) are the compacted, spirally wound membranes that wrap axons, and each internode is one segment of sheath made by a single Schwann cell. Myelin contains proteins such as P0 (myelin protein zero), PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein 22) and MBP (myelin basic protein), and it insulates the axon so that the nerve impulse jumps from one node to the next. In cross-section each myelinated fibre appears as a pale ring around a central axon. Duplication of the PMP22 gene causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A.

Axons are the long, thin processes of neurons that carry impulses away from the cell body, and in a peripheral nerve they run in bundles inside the fascicles. Myelinated axons, such as motor axons and large sensory fibres, conduct faster as their diameter increases, with the fastest reaching about 120 m/s. In cross-section each myelinated axon is the small central dot inside its pale myelin ring. A cut axon degenerates distally, a process known as Wallerian degeneration.

Nodes of Ranvier are the short gaps, about 1 µm long, between successive myelin segments where the axon is left bare. The exposed axon is packed with voltage-gated sodium channels (the pores that generate the impulse, mainly Nav1.6), so the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes, a process called saltatory conduction. In longitudinal sections they show as small breaks between myelin segments. Antibodies against the nodal GM1 ganglioside (a fatty sugar in the membrane) are associated with the acute motor axonal form of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Schwann cell nuclei are the elongated nuclei of the cells that wrap peripheral axons, with one nucleus for each internode of myelin. Each nucleus lies in the thin collar of cytoplasm outside the myelin, so in transverse section it appears as a dark oval just outside the pale myelin ring. Schwannomas, the tumours of these cells, include the bilateral vestibular schwannomas of neurofibromatosis type 2.

Remak Schwann cells are non-myelinating Schwann cells that enclose several thin unmyelinated axons, each axon lying in its own pocket of cytoplasm. The cell and its axons together form a Remak bundle, which carries mostly slow C fibres for pain, temperature, itch and sympathetic outflow. In section a Remak bundle appears as a small cluster of thin fibres with no myelin ring round them.

Unmyelinated axons, or C fibres, are the thinnest nerve fibres, about 0.2-1.5 µm across, and they conduct slowly at roughly 0.5-2 m/s. They carry slow, burning pain, temperature and itch, and they include the postganglionic sympathetic fibres to sweat glands and blood vessels. They usually outnumber the myelinated fibres in mixed nerves, and they are often affected early in small-fibre neuropathy, as in diabetes. In section they appear as thin fibres in Remak bundles (groups of axons sharing one Remak Schwann cell), with no myelin ring.

Endoneurial capillaries are the small blood vessels that run among the nerve fibres inside each fascicle, within the endoneurium. Their endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions, so they form the inner, vascular part of the blood-nerve barrier that keeps blood-borne substances out of the endoneurial fluid. They are fed by arteriolar branches of the vasa nervorum that pierce the perineurium. In section they appear as tiny thin-walled vessels with flattened endothelial nuclei between the myelinated fibres.

Schwann cell outer cytoplasm is the thin outermost layer of Schwann cell cytoplasm, lying between the myelin sheath and the basal lamina. It houses the Schwann cell nucleus and organelles, and it connects with the inner cytoplasm through channels such as the Schmidt-Lanterman incisures, which run through the myelin. In section it appears as a thin rim just outside the myelin ring.

The Schwann basal lamina is the continuous sheet of extracellular matrix that surrounds each Schwann cell, lying just outside its plasma membrane. It is made of laminin, type IV collagen and heparan sulphate proteoglycan, and it guides regrowing axons along the tube left behind after injury, as well as supporting normal myelination. It is usually seen only with electron microscopy or a special stain such as periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), as a thin, dense line around each Schwann cell.

Epineurial fat is the adipose tissue lying between the fascicles of a peripheral nerve, made of lobules of fat cells (adipocytes). It cushions the fascicles against pressure. In section it shows as clusters of clear fat cells between the fascicles. Nerves with little fat in a superficial position, such as the ulnar nerve at the elbow, are the ones most prone to compression injury.

Vasa nervorum (arterioles) are the small arterioles that supply a peripheral nerve, arising from nearby named arteries. In the epineurium they form a longitudinal network along the nerve, and their branches pierce the perineurium to feed the endoneurial capillaries inside each fascicle. In section they appear as small, thick-walled vessels with a well-developed smooth muscle wall, lying in the outer epineurium.

Vasa nervorum (venules) are the small veins of the nerve that collect blood from the capillaries of the endoneurium and perineurium and drain it into the epineurial veins. They run alongside the arterioles in the epineurium. In section they are identified by their thin walls, which lack the thick smooth muscle layer of the arterioles, and by their wide lumen, which often contains red blood cells.
